    Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

    📅 29 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a latest technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.
    • Recent findings suggest that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances.
    • Sources indicate that type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a latest technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

    Recent findings suggest that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

    Sources indicate that type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

    These measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

    It has been revealed that however, there is an vital complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

    How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements.

    Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

    Industry observers note that researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

    A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe.

    The latest framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

    By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

    Recent findings suggest that "A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," states Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most important missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe.".

    Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos.

    It has been revealed that building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

    Sources indicate that the process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

    This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

    Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone.

    One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

    Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

    Industry observers note that according to the researchers, the newly introduced method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially vital because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

    Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge.

    According to recent reports, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, right now being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

    The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

    "Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," states Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

    Insights Into How Supernovae Form.

    According to recent reports, the benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides upcoming information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

    By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

    The researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

    As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a fresh era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

    Materials provided by University of Barcelona. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    • CD Projekt Red notes the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 will be comparable to the one Rockstar made between GTA 5 and GTA 6, with improvements planned for nearly every part of the game.
    • GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.
    • However, the comparison came up again during CD Projekt’s earnings call, when the company was asked whether players should expect a similar leap from its next Witcher game.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CD Projekt Red notes the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 will be comparable to the one Rockstar made between GTA 5 and GTA 6, with improvements planned for nearly every part of the game.

    GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.

    However, the comparison came up again during CD Projekt’s earnings call, when the company was asked whether players should expect a similar leap from its next Witcher game.

    As first reported by Eurogamer, CD Projekt Red co-CEO Michal Nowakowski mentioned the studio had looked at what changed between Rockstar’s two games and that he expected The Witcher 4 to make a comparable jump.

    Recent findings suggest that “We believe there’s going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4, I think so, yes. It’s been 11 years, we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4,” stated Nowakowski.

    Nowakowski was also asked whether GTA 6’s launch would push CD Projekt Red to spend more on its own games. After all, GTA 6 is expected to have exceeded $1 billion in total development costs.

    However, the CD Projekt Red CEO said the studio’s ambitions for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2 had stayed the same.

    “We have certain ambitions when it comes to Witcher [4] and Cyberpunk 2, they have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it’s [that it’s] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that’s for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers,” he added.

    The Witcher 4 dev admits they are worried about living up to Witcher 3.

    CDPR boss hopes The Witcher 4 will win back fans after Cyberpunk 2077’s launch disaster.

    CD Projekt Red reveals major differences between Cyberpunk 2077 & Witcher 3.

    The Witcher 4 is being developed for PlayStation 5, PC, and Xbox Series X/S and is presently targeting a 2028 launch.

    Quantum mechanics once baffled scientists. Now it's changing the world

    📅 05 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science.
    • Industry observers note that in a newly introduced perspective article published in Science, Dr.
    • Industry observers note that "Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

    Industry observers note that in a newly introduced perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

    Industry observers note that "Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago.".

    Sources indicate that scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to newly introduced energy technologies.

    From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology.

    One of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

    Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

    Recent findings suggest that "That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," said Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection.".

    The foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

    Their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

    Quantum Coherence and the Rise of Lasers.

    Industry observers note that among the most notable concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

    It has been revealed that quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

    Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance.".

    Industry observers note that entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

    Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits.

    One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

    Recent findings suggest that traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

    "It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully stated.

    Quantum Biology, Gravity, and Turbulence.

    The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

    In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

    Quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

    Recent findings suggest that researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

    The Next Century of Quantum Discovery.

    Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

    Industry observers note that can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What fresh insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

    Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

    In a recent development, "At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he remarked. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning.".

    Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GTA 6 players who used the Newly introduced Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.
    • With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Newly introduced Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.
    • While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Newly introduced Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 players who used the Newly introduced Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.

    With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Newly introduced Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.

    While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Newly introduced Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.

    Unfortunately, getting into Vice City a few hours early appears to have come with an unexpected drawback.

    As reported by IGN, Rockstar left out the ability to consume cocaine from your inventory in the Australian version of GTA 6, with Newly introduced Zealand reportedly receiving the same version.

    In the international release, players can collect baggies of cocaine or skim some off larger bricks. Consuming cocaine through the item wheel gives players a supercharged stamina bar for roughly 30 seconds.

    Australia’s video game classification rules allow depictions of illicit drug use but prohibit players from receiving gameplay benefits for taking them, even in games rated R18+.

    Interestingly, New Zealand doesn’t have this same restriction, but testing by GTA BOOM found that the mechanic was also absent from its New Zealand playthroughs.

    Players had already suspected GTA 6 was censored in certain regions before launch when dataminers discovered a roughly 700KB discrepancy in the Australian and New Zealand game files.

    Unlike Xbox owners who temporarily changed their console’s location, PS5 players who bought the New Zealand edition still own that regional copy even when playing on their regular account.

    Industry observers note that luckily, those affected aren’t missing out on too much. Adrenaline can still be used to boost stamina and other stats, while scripted sequences involving cocaine remain intact.

    Still, it’s a rather amusing twist that some of GTA 6‘s most impatient fans ended up with less content than those who waited a few extra hours.

    #138801. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

    Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

    📅 13 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence.
    • Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS).
    • It has been revealed that the human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

    Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

    Rethinking How the Brain Makes Decisions.

    It has been revealed that the human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

    Sources indicate that for decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

    Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

    Sources indicate that instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

    Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

    "We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov mentioned. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking.".

    Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity.

    To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

    According to recent reports, the scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

    Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

    Recent findings suggest that "The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov remarked. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further.".

    What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI.

    It has been revealed that the researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

    It has been revealed that next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop latest technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

    It has been revealed that "By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov noted. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these at the moment unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in fresh architectures for AI.".

    Amazon has been expanding its Prime Air delivery service across the US, aiming to reach nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026. However, several crashes involving its drones have attracted the attention of federal regulators.

    Speaking to WXYZ 7 News Detroit, Jim Brennan explained that the drone successfully dropped the package into his backyard before striking a fiber-optic cable and losing one of its propellers.

    The aircraft then veered sideways before becoming trapped between his neighbor’s garage roof and nearby power lines.

    “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan said.

    Logan Coomes, whose garage was struck, mentioned an Amazon Prime Air team arrived within 10 minutes of the crash and worked with local utility workers to remove the drone by early evening.

    The organization reportedly offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave Coomes a $100 Amazon gift card.

    In a statement shared with CNN, an Amazon spokesperson mentioned its Prime Air drones conduct nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered “hundreds of thousands of packages this year.”.

    Amazon also noted the incident marked the first crash of its kind involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit.

    The FAA published a preliminary incident notification on November 23, confirming that it was investigating the crash.

    #138795. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

    📅 14 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1169 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

    📅 14 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J.
    • In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today.
    • According to recent reports, "These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

    In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

    According to recent reports, "These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today.".

    Industry observers note that denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant fresh risks.

    At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

    He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

    Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

    According to recent reports, "Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions.".

    Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

    "Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how').".

    He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

    "A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

    "Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it.".

    Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

    Why Human Knowledge Resists Encoding.

    Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem.".

    According to recent reports, computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

    "Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning indicates. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying.".

    According to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

    "How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it.".

    Context and Culture Shape Intelligence.

    Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

    Industry observers note that context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

    "When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

    Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

    Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

    "Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

    "Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought.".

    AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding.

    Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

    "Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide.".

    It has been revealed that he argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

    According to recent reports, "Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

    Industry observers note that "Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

    According to recent reports, "Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences.".

    Materials provided by Taylor & Francis Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    • As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft confirmed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

    Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The tech giant explains:.

    As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the upcoming private strategy. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

    In a recent development, to Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

    Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business people. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A 16-year-old boy has revealed how a chance encounter in Among Us led to him and his mother helping rescue a teenage girl who had allegedly been held captive for more than 500 days.
    • Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.
    • Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A 16-year-old boy has revealed how a chance encounter in Among Us led to him and his mother helping rescue a teenage girl who had allegedly been held captive for more than 500 days.

    Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.

    Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15. She was allegedly held against her will in the basement of a home in Huntington, Oregon.

    For Colorado teenager Landon Tresp, what began as an ordinary gaming session on October 15 would end with him helping a girl hundreds of miles away escape her alleged captor.

    After meeting in Among Us, Landon and Arellano struck up a friendship and began communicating through Discord.

    “We just kind of clicked,” Landon mentioned.

    Over the following two weeks, Arellano began opening up about her situation, eventually sending Landon news articles covering her disappearance.

    Realizing something was seriously wrong, Landon turned to his mother, Khristina, for help on Halloween. Neither knew that within 24 hours, the girl would finally be free.

    Khristina began speaking with Arellano through Discord, but locating the teenager proved challenging as she didn’t know the address where she was being held.

    “I knew I had to do everything I could to make sure she was brought to safety and had a second chance,” Khristina recalled.

    It has been revealed that determined to find her, Khristina searched online property records before turning to real estate website Zillow. After being sent photos of two potential houses, Arellano recognized the second property.

    Teenage girl held captive for 500 days rescued after secretly asking for help in Among Us.

    Among Us hackers targeted as InnerSloth rush out emergency hotfix.

    World of Warcraft account helps police locate missing 16-year-old.

    Khristina contacted the girl’s family and began working with the FBI to bring her home.

    Speaking with KOAA, Khristina described how devastating it was to learn just how long Arellano had been missing.

    “Just heartbreaking to think that she had been going through what she had for over 520 days and without anyone that she could reach a hand out to and not knowing where you’re at,” she mentioned.

    On November 1, authorities arrived at the Oregon residence. Khristina stayed on a video call with Arellano, encouraging her to make the final few steps toward freedom.

    Sources indicate that “I was on the video chat with her when I told her to face those basement stairs and run up them and down that hallway,” Khristina recalled. “And grab that front door because that was her freedom.”.

    After more than 500 days away from home, Arellano was finally in the care of law enforcement and was taken for medical treatment and evaluation.

    For Landon, seeing the friend he had met just weeks earlier finally reach safety was an overwhelming moment.

    “Oh my God, just pure bliss. I was so happy she was safe in that car. I was so happy she was out of that horrible monster’s house,” he noted.

    Sources indicate that adam Hunter Harmel, 39, has since been indicted on a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Prosecutors allege he met the girl online before traveling to Utah and taking her across state lines.

    Despite everything that happened, Landon and Arellano haven’t stopped playing video games together.

    The pair remain friends, while Khristina continues to speak with Arellano every day. The family is also hoping to meet her in person.

    What began with two strangers meeting in Among Us has become a friendship that extends far beyond the game, with Landon and his mother giving Arellano the help she had desperately needed for more than a year.

    #138791. Fresh programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

    📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1400 w)

    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Fresh programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

    📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
    • The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
    • Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

    The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

    Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.

    In a recent development, the rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

    According to recent reports, these challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

    In a recent development, however, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

    It has been revealed that to address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

    The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

    Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait.

    Industry observers note that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information promptly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

    Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

    One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

    CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

    Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility.

    Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

    For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

    That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever latest capabilities are needed.

    Sources indicate that the problem is especially vital for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

    A Programmable Design for Controlling Light.

    The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

    It has been revealed that together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

    Using the latest CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

    This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

    Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape.

    Recent findings suggest that the researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

    This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

    Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

    The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

    Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical.

    The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

    They also evaluated a range of real-world problems that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

    The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

    One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions.

    The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

    Recent findings suggest that the design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

    These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

    The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

    Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers.

    If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

    In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

    This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

    Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

    Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

    Researchers Strategy Larger Programmable Photonic Systems.

    Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a fresh design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.".

    It has been revealed that co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We strategy to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.".

    Sources indicate that dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is at the moment conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

    It has been revealed that ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

    The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

    Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over $60,000 has been raised to help cover the vet bills of a beloved railway station cat in England after he suddenly fell ill.

    On November 23, a 12-year-old ginger cat known for greeting passengers at a train station in the UK was taken to the vet after his family noticed he was eating less and sleeping more than usual.

    While George’s family is still waiting to find out what made their beloved pet unwell, feline fans from across the globe have shown their support by raising thousands of dollars to help with his treatment.

    “George has brought so much happiness, laughter and comfort to so many people over the years, and now we’re doing everything we can to get him back to his happy, healthy self,” reads a post on the station cat’s Facebook page.

    “We know times are difficult for so many, and your kind messages, love and good wishes mean more than you could possibly imagine…Thank you for loving our gorgeous ginger boy as much as we do. We’re keeping everything crossed for him.”.

    In a post shared on George’s GoFundMe page, his family revealed that the cat’s medical bill has already reached $1,958 (£1,500), and mentioned that further investigations into the cat’s health could lead to further costs.

    Recent findings suggest that however, since posting the campaign, George has received an outpouring of donations to help cover the costs. As of November 25, the cute cat has raised $60,582 (£46,393) of his $78,000 (£60,000) goal, much to the shock of his owners.

    “We are completely overwhelmed and incredibly humbled by the love, kindness and generosity that has been shown towards our little ginger boy,” noted George’s social media manager Simone Carter.

    “When we set up this fundraiser, we could never have imagined the response it would receive. From the bottom of our hearts, thank you to every single person who has donated, shared the appeal, or taken the time to send George their love and good wishes.”.

    George’s family has pledged to use any money left over after his medical bills are paid to help other cats in need.

    “George has spent so many years bringing a little happiness into people’s lives, and it is incredibly moving to see just how much love is being returned to him,” noted Carter.

    “How wonderful that, through George, we will also be able to make a difference to the lives of other cats who need a little kindness and a helping hand.”.

    #138786. Latest Update: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

    📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1393 w)

    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

    📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment.
    • It has been revealed that MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts.
    • Sources indicate that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond promptly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

    It has been revealed that MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

    Sources indicate that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

    It has been revealed that the MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

    A Smaller Lidar System With a Wider View.

    The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

    Industry observers note that "The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

    Industry observers note that the study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

    How Lidar Maps Its Surroundings.

    Sources indicate that many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

    According to recent reports, silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

    According to recent reports, at the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

    Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

    Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

    When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

    "This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

    In a recent development, the unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

    To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

    Three Antenna Shapes Reduce Interference.

    It has been revealed that in a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

    It has been revealed that the MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

    "Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto claims.

    Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way.

    Sources indicate that reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

    The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

    Sources indicate that each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

    According to recent reports, "We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

    Recent findings suggest that the researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

    Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

    Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent.

    In a recent development, under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

    The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

    The researchers now initiative to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

    It has been revealed that "This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

    Sources indicate that the Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

    Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rockstar Games has revealed several features that were scrapped during the development of GTA 6, including activities that were available in previous Grand Theft Auto games.

    According to recent reports, after years of anticipation, GTA 6 has finally arrived, introducing players to Leonida alongside the franchise’s newest protagonists, Jason and Lucia. The game has also earned a Metacritic score of 99, matching The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

    However, despite the number of activities available throughout the open world, Rockstar has revealed that several planned gameplay mechanics and returning features never made it into the finished game.

    Speaking to German outlet PC Games, Rockstar North development manager Rob Nelson and design producer Scott Mitchell discussed several features that were considered during development but ultimately abandoned.

    Industry observers note that among them was tennis, which players could participate in throughout GTA 5. Rockstar had planned to bring the activity back for GTA 6, but its implementation failed to meet the developer’s standards. Mini golf, however, made it into the finished game.

    GTA 6 features that were cut, per a PC Games interview with Rob Nelson and Scott Mitchell of Rockstar North:Tennis (planned, but didn't meet Rockstar's standards)Cinema and theatre visits (not interactive enough)CrawlingHome decoratingCraftingSource:… pic.twitter.com/NviyEdt2M9.

    Industry observers note that the developers also revealed that players were originally going to be able to crawl, decorate their homes, and craft items. These mechanics were ultimately scrapped, with some not fitting the game’s story or gameplay.

    Cinema and theater visits were also removed, as Rockstar felt the activities were not interactive enough.

    Nelson also explained how Red Dead Redemption 2 influenced the development of GTA 6, particularly when it came to storytelling and the relationship between its two protagonists.

    The Western’s approach to pacing encouraged Rockstar to incorporate quieter moments into GTA 6, giving Jason and Lucia more opportunities for character development between the game’s action sequences.

    The top smartphone brands in the United States include Apple, Samsung, Motorola, and Google Pixel in that order. Apple continues to absolutely dominate at a whopping 57% market share in Q3 2026, up from 50% during the same period last year.

    • Sources indicate that many parents struggle with the idea of getting a smartphone for their kids.
    • Both watches are on sale well ahead of Black Friday, too!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Garmin and Bark are competing for your money this year, and these sales make it easy to get something fun that’ll keep your kids safe and in touch.

    Sources indicate that many parents struggle with the idea of getting a smartphone for their kids. If you want your kids to stay in touch but not have access to all the garbage on the internet, a smartwatch is the best alternative. I’ve tested a lot of kids’ smartwatches over the years, and I can easily recommend the two in the picture above: the Bark Watch and the Garmin Bounce 2.

    Both watches are on sale well ahead of Black Friday, too! The Bark Watch is $11 off at Amazon ($274 total) and $50 off at Bark, while the Garmin Bounce 2 is $50-$64 off (starting at $235) depending on the color you choose. The least expensive Garmin Bounce 2 is the blue color in the photo I took above, which my son loved.

    According to recent reports, choosing between the two is easy enough. Garmin’s watch is the least complicated and comes in a slightly more durable case with fun colors. It’s slightly cheaper than Bark, but doesn’t have any health sensors on board. It mainly tracks steps, allows your kids to message or call you, and gives you geofencing and location tracking through a $9.99 per month LTE subscription strategy. It’s got a 5ATM rating and a polycarbonate case, so it’s quite durable.

    It has been revealed that the Garmin Bounce 2 is preloaded with a few mini games and educational apps, plus the Garmin Jr. app has built-in unlockables and rewards parents can set for doing chores, completing schoolwork, etc. Battery life is roughly 2 days with normal use, but can be less if you’re in an area with poor LTE reception. The Garmin Bounce 2 is best for kids 10 and under.

    Industry observers note that the Bark Watch uses Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 hardware and a custom version of Wear OS. It’s a much more powerful watch and only gets a day of battery life because of it. This one feels like a midpoint between a kids’ watch and a standard Wear OS watch, as it has all the power of Wear OS but doesn’t feature the Google Play Store. It doesn’t have any games, social media, or browsers.

    It has been revealed that since it uses Samsung’s hardware, it includes cutting-edge health sensors that your kids can use, plus great multitasking and a svelte, attractive design. Bark charges $15 per month for its proposal, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online.     📅 14 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (839 w)

    Latest Update: World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

    📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
    • Industry observers note that scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles.
    • In a recent development, the experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

    Industry observers note that scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

    In a recent development, the experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

    A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World.

    It has been revealed that conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

    The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

    It has been revealed that operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an key objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

    The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

    Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero.

    Industry observers note that to make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

    "In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

    The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

    "Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

    Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

    "This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.

    Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware.

    According to recent reports, the researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

    Recent findings suggest that that capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

    "Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.

    Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

    The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

    Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

    Sources indicate that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

    Last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery revision detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

    Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

    It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

    Recent findings suggest that the post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and users are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese Fresh Year.

    In an act of good faith, Clicks says it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

    It has been revealed that A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.
