    #138741. TSMC’s $22.6 billion Texas initiative wouldn’t make 2nm-or-better chips until 2031

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1874 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    TSMC’s $22.6 billion Texas initiative wouldn’t make 2nm-or-better chips until 2031

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TSMC has made an application for a new fab and campus near College Station, Brazos County, Texas.
    • In a recent development, this would be the company’s “second campus” for advanced chipmaking in the U.S.
    • TSMC is looking to build out more in the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TSMC has made an application for a new fab and campus near College Station, Brazos County, Texas. The proposed fab would be just one county over from Terafab, would likely share supply chains, and would be positioned to make 2nm-class chips by 2031, with the $22.6 billion blueprint detailing how the Taiwanese chipmaker is planning to expand its U.S. operations. An application under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program for a school property-tax limit demonstrates TSMC is weighing a new fab site. The fab wouldn’t make 2nm or more advanced chips until 2031, six years after 2nm volume production began in Taiwan. It would come with a school-tax break valued at around $354 million.

    In a recent development, this would be the company’s “second campus” for advanced chipmaking in the U.S. and the first outside Arizona. The Comptroller has recommended the tax application for approval, which the school district and the governor still have to grant. The application comes from TSMC Arizona Corporation, which is TSMC’s subsidiary located in Phoenix. Construction is projected to start in 2027, but the plan remains under evaluation, and nothing in the filing commits TSMC to buy the land or to build on it.

    TSMC is looking to build out more in the U.S. because most of its large customers are based there and the government has been “very helpful” in pursuing additional fab capacity, Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said in October. Texas is one option for expanding beyond Arizona, though the filing doesn’t say what drew TSMC there. TSMC judges each site on its tax environment, workforce availability, utility capacity and cost, and site and infrastructure readiness, as well as its “long-term scalability and expansion potential.” TSMC indicates Arizona offers “established operational efficiencies and lower capital risk,” and that the tax incentive would aid this further.

    According to recent reports, TSMC has “nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress,” Wei stated on the October earnings call, including 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan and “another five to six fabs overseas.” Annual capacity for its 2nm (N2) family is expected to more than double in 2027. TSMC also expects more of its fabs to be ramping up in the U.S.

    Recent findings suggest that texas wouldn’t begin commercial operations until 2031, and the economic model filed with the proposal doesn’t have it at full operations until 2032. By contrast, the second fab in Arizona is expected to begin volume production in Q3 2027, but at 3nm. In Taiwan, N2 has been in high-volume production since Q4 2025. TSMC expects A14, its next full node after N2, to enter risk production in 2027 and volume in 2028. By 2031, A14 is set to have been in volume production for about three years, so a Texas fab that starts on 2nm would be at least a generation behind TSMC’s leading edge. Taiwan has also debated limits on how advanced TSMC’s overseas fabs can be.

    A16 (a 2nm-family node) volume production.

    3nm volume production, second fab.

    2nm “and/or more advanced,” commercial operations.

    The new site would have one or more fabs but, as it stands, Brazos County’s announcement describes one. For scale, we’ve estimated that a single 2nm-class module with about 20,000 wafer starts a month costs $25 billion to $35 billion, so this strategy’s $22.6 billion budget falls below the low end of that range.

    The price tag is split in multiple ways, with $8.60 billion for buildings and other real property, while 62% of the total, or $14.02 billion, is for tooling, machinery and equipment, a category that on the filing’s list also covers power, HVAC, cleanroom, water and gas systems. The building's spending would come first, in 2027, 2028, and 2029 alone. Tool spending would begin in that last year and peak at $9.05 billion in 2030, with about 65% of the tool budget landing in that year, before ending at $963.9 million in 2032 — the form’s Schedule A stops at 2031 and $21.66 billion total.

    In a recent development, the tool spending schedule lines up with a change in how TSMC prints its chips. Lithography, the step in the chipmaking process that uses light to project circuit patterns onto the wafer, requires advanced machines. The most advanced do it with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light. High-NA EUV tools have a higher numerical aperture, gathering more light to print finer features in one pass. Wei noted TSMC intends to use High-NA in 2030, which matches the 2030 peak in Texas tool spending, but that is a firm-wide strategy, and nothing in the Texas plan gives a delivery schedule or names High-NA tools specifically.

    What the plan does spell out is its list of eligible property: fab and central utility plant buildings, cleanroom systems, ultra-pure water and wastewater treatment with water-reclaim systems, bulk and specialty gas as well as automated material handling, and gas-insulated switchgear.

    Also named is mask or reticle shop equipment as well as lithography, etch, deposition, implant, chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), diffusion, and clean/wet tools, by type, although the list names no tool vendors, EUV counts, or wafer capacity. The mask shop is highlighted as “co-located within the fab and integral to the manufacturing process.” Masks are patterned plates used by a lithography tool to project their patterns onto each wafer, one per chip layer, and every new design needs its own set. Making them on site suggests the fab is meant to stand on its own. Wei also stated TSMC is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031, which is the year the Texas site would open.

    It has been revealed that the plan’s location is in Brazos County, Texas, sited across 86 parcels and almost 3,232 acres of land, which is about five square miles. This compares to TSMC’s Phoenix campus at about 1,078 acres on the county tax roll, with about 902 more purchased in January; this leaves the Texas site at about 1.6 times that total. TSMC would build and manage the site, which sets it apart from Terafab, a fab a TSMC customer is planning one county over: Wei has confirmed talks about using its capacity but said any such fab would have to be run by TSMC.

    It has been revealed that residents in development areas for fabs and data centers tend to raise two concerns, and both are related to utility usage. The first is power: a local report states Bryan Texas Utilities provides that for the proposed area, but it’s unclear who would serve the fab. For scale, a utility filing in Arizona reportedly puts TSMC’s built-out Phoenix campus at about 1.9 gigawatts, a figure for the whole campus, not a single fab.

    According to recent reports, the second is water: Wellborn Special Utility District reportedly provides service, while the developer is said to intend to buy its water from a third party instead. As a comparison, a state document on an unnamed firm’s $45 billion, two-fab project in Sherman, as reported by the Dallas Business Journal, lists 8 to 10 million gallons a day to start with a peak at 20 to 25 million after buildout, but this isn’t a 1:1. That project is targeting production in Q4 2029.

    Recent findings suggest that economic impacts are a significant part of the deal: the strategy projects 2,099 direct jobs by 2030, while the agreement would require only 35, the legal minimum. Pay, on the other hand, comes with a projected average salary nearly double the wage level that would need clearing.

    Texas appears willing to work with TSMC on this, with a recommendation for approval signed by Deputy Comptroller Noah Betz this week. The gross tax benefit would build over 14 years, starting four years before the formal incentive period, and would cut the district’s maintenance and operations (M&O) levy on the project nearly in half. Even so, the full $354.1 million is only 1.6% of the $22.6 billion investment. In return, TSMC would have to post a performance bond equal to 10% of the benefit.

    The Comptroller believes the incentive is a compelling factor — TSMC would not invest in Texas without it — but the office indicates it has not audited or verified the organization’s projections. TSMC, for its part, calls the limit “determinative.”.

    Jobs the agreement would require.

    $135,687 in 2028, rising 2% a year.

    Minimum average wage for the project’s jobs.

    Construction workers, 2027–2029.

    9,841 a year on average; 18,134 at the 2029 peak.

    708 a year; average stay 41 days.

    Tax benefit during construction, 2028–2031.

    Tax benefit in the incentive period, 2032–2041.

    School M&O tax over 20 years, without the agreement.

    School M&O tax over 20 years, with the agreement.

    In a recent development, A potentially far larger incentive is federal: a tax credit worth 35 cents back to every qualifying dollar spent, as long as construction technically begins before the end of the year. “Qualified” means the cost of the fab’s depreciable physical property that is integral to running the fab, meaning the buildings and the tools, in the year each goes into service, and “construction” means actual physical work of a significant nature or paying or incurring at least 5% of the qualifying property’s cost, with work continuing afterward. Construction here is projected to start in 2027, after that cutoff, though off-site work under a binding written contract or early spending this year could still count, and an extension has been proposed in the Senate.

    Recent findings suggest that the land doesn’t count in this equation, and neither does office space. This is also a credit off the tax bill, dollar for dollar, not a deduction. The rate was 25% under the 2022 CHIPS Act and rose to 35% for property placed in service after 2025. If the full $22.6 billion qualified, that would be about $7.9 billion back, but not every dollar qualifies.

    If Texas doesn’t work out, TSMC is also considering “a latest land parcel in Arizona,” which would be closer to the existing North Phoenix site. TSMC says that may make many things easier, such as handling a workforce and the logistics, with the ability to use existing suppliers and relationships on known infrastructure. This is an incentive for the state of Texas to give the tax break.

    Recent findings suggest that the tax agreement needs approval from both the College Station ISD board and the governor. The district also owns one of the parcels on TSMC’s list for the site: almost 91 acres, with a 24,496-square-foot building from 2024. The board has set a public hearing for Dec. 10, with public comment, and could approve the project’s reinvestment zone that day.

    In a recent development, the district has 30 days from the day it receives the application, which puts its deadline in late December. As for Brazos County, town halls could reportedly begin as early as the first week of December, though the county has promised only one, “in the near future.”.

    Assuming things move forward, the real measure begins with the first phase on land. Even if production arrives a generation late, it would be a positive development for U.S.-based chipmaking.

    Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

    📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
    • It has been revealed that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy.
    • In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

    It has been revealed that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

    In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

    "The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a latest generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," states DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

    Sources indicate that mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

    Using Light Inside Computer Chips.

    Recent findings suggest that much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

    Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

    Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

    Recent findings suggest that the compact DTU nanolaser is an crucial step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

    Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers.

    The upcoming nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

    It has been revealed that at its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

    In a recent development, when researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

    The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

    Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use.

    Recent findings suggest that the next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

    Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

    In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

    Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

    Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

    The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these upcoming Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

    “Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

    The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

    While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for key apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

    “Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

    In a recent development, over in China, this has been the case for a few years with a leopard known as Pan Baobao. The 19-year-old leopard has gone viral a few times now, especially for his resemblance to Officer Clawhauser from the Zootopia franchise.

    It has been revealed that keepers at the Panzhihua Zoo have, over the years, attempted to help the chunky predator lose a few pounds by changing his diet and getting him moving more. However, with the latest year approaching, they’ve decided to put an end to those attempts.

    Keepers have noted that the big cat is in “good condition,” and they just want to provide a comfortable life for Pan Baobao, who is still in “healthy spirits” too.

    #138736. AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

    📅 13 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1531 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

    📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a fresh way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs.
    • The study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit owners.
    • The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a fresh way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

    The study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit owners. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

    The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

    "Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that indicates that the method is picking up a real signal," claims Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them.".

    What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials.

    Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify notable safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

    "Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns.".

    The distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

    According to recent reports, "We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit consumers in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating.".

    Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal.

    The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet consumers to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

    Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

    "Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," indicates Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report.".

    In a recent development, since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

    Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more promptly when millions of people begin using a drug.

    In a recent development, "Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," claims Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight.".

    AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible.

    One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

    Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

    It has been revealed that patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

    Recent findings suggest that researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

    Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

    Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and rapidly.

    "Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," states Sehgal.

    Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts.

    In a recent development, the researchers stress that Reddit customers do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

    Even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

    About 44% of users included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.

    More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

    It has been revealed that nearly 4% of owners who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

    Consumers also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

    Fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

    Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting.

    One possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely key region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

    "These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically.".

    Industry observers note that the researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

    Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads.

    For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

    "They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," says Sehgal.

    Industry observers note that the researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

    "We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 owners globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar says.

    In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

    Sources indicate that that could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread swiftly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among users may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

    "The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move rapidly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," notes Guntuku.

    According to recent reports, this study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

    • President Donald Trump says that he could pardon returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he finds himself in legal hot water over his already-admitted affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed employee and an alleged Chinese spy.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump says that he could pardon returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he finds himself in legal hot water over his already-admitted affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed employee and an alleged Chinese spy. The Nvidia founder has since admitted to the organization's board that he had more affairs than those already reported, including one with a direct report.

    Huang is set to meet with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next week and will be expected to answer questions about the affair, its effect on Nvidia, and how it impacts the national security of the country as a whole. Trump pushed for Huang's reinstatement, going so far as to pressure the Nvidia board via a telephone call. With that in mind, a NY Post report that he could consider pardoning Huang may not be all that surprising.

    It has been revealed that discussing Huang's meeting on December 1, Trump argued that the two-time Nvidia CEO doesn't need to worry about pleading the Fifth Amendment to avoid incriminating himself. Instead, Trump says, the whole saga is "an interesting story for people,” suggesting that perhaps the American people will learn more in the future. “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know, a very smart person,” Trump noted of the man whose mistress is also married to an alleged Chinese spy herself.

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang passed information about Nvidia to Chinese officials during her affair with Jensen Huang (no relation). The good news, it seems, is that Trump is of the understanding that Alice Huang is the only woman Jensen was having an affair with who also has links to China's Ministry of State Security.

    When pushed on the potential for a pardon for Huang if he was found to have broken any laws, Trump admitted that “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.” The news will no doubt be music to the ears of Huang, with lawmakers expected to give him a grilling and some already not expecting him to be forthcoming in terms of the answers he offers to their questions.     The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

    📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics.
    • It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics.
    • The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to fresh ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

    It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

    The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

    The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

    According to recent reports, familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

    In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

    Sources indicate that "What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," claims lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

    Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

    To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

    Industry observers note that when laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

    Recent findings suggest that chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

    "We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

    Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

    The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

    Industry observers note that when the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This highlighted that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

    Sources indicate that "These results open a upcoming direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

    From Abstract Mathematics to Newly introduced Optical Physics.

    The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

    It has been revealed that more broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover fresh ways to control and study light.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A woman in Germany was slapped with a €25 ($27 USD) fine after sitting down on a bench at a children’s playground to cry, unaware that she was breaking the law by being there without a child.

    The 31-year-old woman, identified as Hana, had gone for a walk through Glückaufpark in Gelsenkirchen on October 25 to clear her head after becoming overwhelmed by financial and academic pressures.

    The chemistry student eventually broke down in tears, taking a seat on a bench at the playground and calling her aunt.

    “I just wanted to be alone and not be seen by anyone,” she told German broadcaster WDR.

    Industry observers note that however, three municipal enforcement officers approached her and asked whether two boys playing on the swings were her children. When she mentioned no, the officers demanded her identification and issued her a €25 fine.

    Under Gelsenkirchen’s municipal regulations, playgrounds are reserved for children aged 14 and under, along with their parents, guardians, and supervisors.

    While there was a sign outlining the playground’s rules, BILD reports that it did not explicitly state that unaccompanied adults were prohibited from sitting on the benches.

    Hana argued that the officers could have simply asked her to move instead of issuing a fine.

    “I felt as though I was worth nothing as a human being,” she said.

    Despite criticism, the city defended the officers’ actions, describing the fine as relatively mild and proportionate. According to WELT, Hana has since paid the fine to avoid incurring additional costs.

    Rather than relaxing the rules, the city council discussed increasing the maximum penalty for playground violations from €55 to €60 ($66) on November 17.

    MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
    • Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
    • According to recent reports, researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a latest approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

    Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

    According to recent reports, researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a latest approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

    Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

    The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

    Industry observers note that "We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," states Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

    According to recent reports, chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

    AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

    Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

    The team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

    The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

    For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

    A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

    To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

    Sources indicate that "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How states.

    Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers.

    The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

    Recent findings suggest that although this method requires substantial computing power, it can blueprint difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

    Industry observers note that repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each upcoming flip under the proper conditions.

    In a recent development, "If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

    The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

    In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate rapidly enough for real-time flight.

    A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

    "The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

    During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

    In a recent development, experiments indicated that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

    It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

    "This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up latest opportunities for multimodal locomotion," indicates Hsiao.

    The team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

    "This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

    Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

    One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

    The team also plans to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

    "For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a latest control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

    This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life.
    • Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.
    • According to recent reports, lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many challenges with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

    Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

    According to recent reports, lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

    In a recent development, understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

    Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

    Industry observers note that the problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

    That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

    I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

    I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very rapidly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

    In a recent development, google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

    Recent findings suggest that the Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

    In a recent development, videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

    On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a substantial uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

    With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

    Sources indicate that A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

    Despite the massive crackdown, it seems that development is simply moving away from the public platform into private spaces. PortWatch VI, a website tracking the work on unofficial GTA VI PC ports, is right now following 30 projects, with one of the more successful ones reportedly playing for over 90 minutes on an RTX 3050 GPU without any crashes, albeit at an unplayable 1 to 3 FPS. There’s also a post on the r/FitGirlRepack subreddit claiming that an unofficial port could already hit 30 FPS, with the developers working on it targeting 60 FPS within the next three days. They also expect to release the source code within the same time frame.

    Porting games to other platforms used to be a difficult, time-intensive job, but the proliferation of AI tools has made it so much easier (although still requiring skill and effort). This is why one game decompilation hub froze its leaderboard, which had turned into a hollow numbers game as teams rushed to ship PC buggy or laggy PC ports. Anthropic has also taken steps to prevent Claude from being used for video game cloning and reverse-engineering, but independent developers could use other AI tools, like locally run open-weight models, to do the job for them.

    Industry observers note that there have been rumors that Rockstar will launch the game on PC as early as the first quarter of 2027, a massive improvement over the 18-month delay PC gamers had to endure with the previous installment. Rockstar’s parent company certainly wants to recoup the over $2 billion spent on developing the game, and having it available to the millions of PC gamers would certainly help with that goal. But the power that AI has given to developers to allow them to make unofficial ports much more promptly than before is certainly adding to the pressure.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

    📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
    • Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
    • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," mentioned Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a upcoming way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

    Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

    "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," mentioned Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.

    A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

    Industry observers note that the strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

    Quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

    To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The new results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

    "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," noted Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

    Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

    Sources indicate that ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

    These anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

    "The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

    Recent findings suggest that each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

    Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

    Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

    In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

    That experiment demonstrated that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

    Industry observers note that "In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," noted Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

    Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

    For the new study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

    Industry observers note that the S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

    The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

    The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

    By combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

    Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

    "It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," noted Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

    Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

    The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

    According to recent reports, the experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

    "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen mentioned.

    The next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on upcoming techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

    In competitive shooters like Counter-Strike 2, Valorant, and Call of Duty, every millisecond counts. Players are constantly looking for ways to get an edge, whether that’s upgrading their PC, tweaking settings, or investing in a faster monitor.

    Industry observers note that but while graphics cards usually get most of the attention, your monitor plays a huge role in how smooth and responsive a game feels. After all, there’s only so much benefit to pushing hundreds of frames per second if your display can’t keep up.

    With gaming monitors now hitting 480Hz and beyond, refresh rates are reaching some pretty astonishing numbers. But you might be asking, can you actually feel the difference, and is upgrading from 144Hz or 240Hz really worth it?

    In competitive shooters, where quick reactions and precise aiming matter, a monitor’s refresh rate can influence how smoothly movement appears on screen.

    Sources indicate that A higher refresh rate allows the display to revision its image more frequently. For example, a 144Hz monitor refreshes approximately every 6.94 milliseconds, while a 480Hz display refreshes every 2.08 milliseconds.

    That difference can help players track moving opponents and receive updated visual information sooner, particularly in fast-paced games like Counter-Strike 2 and Valorant.

    However, the benefits become smaller at higher refresh rates, and players need a PC capable of producing enough frames to take full advantage of them.

    Refresh rate isn’t the only factor affecting motion clarity, either. OLED panels generally offer much faster pixel response times than traditional LCD monitors, reducing the ghosting that can appear behind moving objects.

    Why you should upgrade to an OLED for GTA 6.

    The best gaming monitor in 2024: Budget, 4K & Ultrawide.

    The best refresh rate for Counter-Strike 2.

    GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE lineup combines those fast response times with high refresh rates, offering different options depending on how players use their monitors.

    Recent findings suggest that the AORUS FO32U24G features a 32-inch fourth-generation Tandem WOLED panel with a 0.03ms GTG response time. Its Dual Mode technology allows players to switch between two display configurations:.

    This approach could appeal to players who regularly switch between different genres. Someone playing Counter-Strike 2 might prefer the 480Hz mode, while a player enjoying a visually demanding single-player game could switch back to 4K.

    The smaller AORUS FO27Q28G takes a different approach, offering a 27-inch QHD Tandem WOLED panel with a 280Hz refresh rate and the same advertised 0.03ms GTG response time.

    Both monitors also support NVIDIA G-SYNC compatibility and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, which can help reduce tearing when frame rates fluctuate.

    Refresh rate and response time aren’t the only specifications to focus on.

    Modern gaming monitors increasingly include built-in features designed to give players more control over visibility, screen layout, and the information displayed during gameplay.

    GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE monitors include several Tactical Features intended for different competitive scenarios:.

    Some of these features may be particularly relevant to Counter-Strike 2 players, many of whom have specific preferences for screen size, resolution, and aspect ratio.

    Tactical Switch 2.0 allows players to change between different display configurations without manually adjusting every setting, while Tactical HUD could be useful in games where players regularly need to reference mini-maps or other on-screen information.

    GIGABYTE also includes Night Vision and AI Black Equalizer to improve visibility in darker environments, alongside Ultra Clear, which uses black-frame insertion to reduce perceived motion blur.

    According to recent reports, not every feature will be useful to every player, and some display-side assists may be restricted under competitive tournament rules. Players should check the rules of the games and competitions they participate in before using them.

    Although 480Hz monitors offer extremely frequent display updates, not every competitive player needs the highest available refresh rate.

    For someone upgrading from a 60Hz or 75Hz display, even moving to 144Hz can make a substantial difference in perceived smoothness.

    Players already using 240Hz or 280Hz monitors may notice a smaller improvement when switching to 480Hz, particularly if their PC struggles to maintain the frame rates required to take advantage of it.

    It has been revealed that A 480Hz monitor makes the most sense for players who prioritize competitive performance and have a PC capable of producing extremely high frame rates. For others, a 280Hz OLED may provide a better balance between responsiveness, resolution, and everyday use.

    GIGABYTE’s M series offers several alternatives depending on panel technology, screen finish, and gaming preferences:.

    The MO27Q2A provides a QD-OLED alternative for players who want fast response times and high refresh rates, while the MO27Q28G and MO27Q28GR offer different screen finishes depending on the environment.

    The M27UP takes a different approach with an IPS panel, making it an option for players who want 4K gaming and high-refresh competitive performance without moving to OLED.

    For players considering OLED, long-term panel care is another factor worth keeping in mind.

    Industry observers note that competitive shooters frequently display static interface elements, including health bars, ammunition counters, mini-maps, and scoreboards. Over extended periods, these elements can contribute to uneven pixel wear.

    GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE FO32U24G and FO27Q28G feature AI OLED Care Pro, which includes automated pixel cleaning, brightness adjustments, and display protection designed to reduce burn-in risk.

    The MO27Q2A, MO27Q28G, and MO27Q28GR instead feature AI OLED Care, providing background panel maintenance and protection.

    While 480Hz OLED monitors represent a high-performance option for competitive gaming, they aren’t necessarily the right choice for everyone.

    Players who spend most of their time in Counter-Strike 2 or Valorant and have PCs capable of producing hundreds of frames per second may benefit from the additional responsiveness.

    For those who split their time between competitive shooters and visually demanding single-player games, a lower-refresh OLED with higher resolution may make more sense.

    Ultimately, the best gaming monitor isn’t always the one with the highest refresh rate. It’s the one that matches the games you play, the hardware you own, and the experience you’re trying to achieve.

    According to recent reports, did anything notable happen this week? Not that I can remember. The weather was quite rainy - will that do? I'm just being silly, of course. We've had - and I suppose are still having - an historic week in video games, as Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives. It's dominated everything and I fear it's going to dominate this article too. But a reminder: next week is our "Not-GTA Week", so we'll be making a concerted effort to talk about games, probably smaller games, that aren't Godzilla blockbusters.

    Recent findings suggest that as you know, this is our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week. This week, rather a lot of us have been playing GTA 6, as you can imagine, and discovering various things about it. But not all of us. Connor, ever the contrarian, has been continuing his race to level 60 in World of Warcraft: Forever, and he's agonisingly close to getting there.

    But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

    According to recent reports, it probably comes as no surprise that I'm - much like the rest of the world - playing GTA 6 right now. While I found Chapter 1 to be quite a slow start, and where I felt somewhat restricted, I've now started Chapter 2 and found myself enjoying stealing cars, jamming along to the radio, and simply exploring Leonida - and all the strange happenings that come with it. There's so much to see and do!

    I'm looking forward to deviating from the main missions for a while to do a spot of bird-watching (I like birds a lot, alright) and seeing what other side activities Leonida has to offer outside of the criminal lifestyle at the core of things. I'm also trying to be the best partner possible to both Jason and Lucia, but I'm itching to cause a bit of trouble soon... Hurting NPCs comes with so much guilt this time around though!

    It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard. It's a perfect Eurogamer game, right? Right? GTA 6's in-game lampoon of Jonathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck and - weirdly - Mark Z. Danielewski is a wonderful bit of top-shelf pastiche. It goes to show just how much fun Rockstar had making GTA 6, and the freedom its dev team had to install as much depth and satire in just about every nook and cranny conceivable. Don't sleep on Tenebrae Lux, it's genuinely satisfying to complete.

    I'm not, historically, the biggest GTA fan - although I've absolutely got a soft spot for Vice City's sublime mood - so I wasn't quite as excited to play GTA 6 as some. But it took, oh I dunno, about 30 seconds before I was sold. This thing has style. And everything else a billion dollars and some incredible development talent gets you. And it's those because-we-can details that have, in my first few hours, left the biggest impression. I spent a good five minutes just marveling at Jason dance - specifically the way his little stationary wiggle (perfectly timed to the radio beat!) shifts seamlessly into a wiggle-strut when you hit the forward button.

    In a recent development, I love the way the setting sun seems to shine just right through the clouds when the moment calls, and those perfect needle drops. And careening through the night - amid the driving rain and smear of taillights, Kylie classic Spinning Around booming on the radio and Jason rocking a recently acquired, slightly improbable hat - this extravagant, ridiculous thing had me completely transfixed. I'm genuinely, unexpectedly excited to see where it takes me next.

    According to recent reports, assuming there's lots of Grand Theft Auto 6 in this article, I'll save you from my own early impressions of this week's blockbuster release. Instead, you get more tales from an MMO. It is what it is!

    I'm level 58 right now, pushing my way into the endgame dungeons. I've almost maxed all my professions, and am gradually getting gear that should serve me well when the raids are added next month.

    Recent findings suggest that but forget all that. I got a salt shaker! As a leatherworker, you can buy a salt shaker from engineers for a little bit of gold on the auction house. These are more vital than you'd assume. With them you can make one refined deeprock salt every three days - a high-end crafting material. Rather than hoard these for fancy gear, I just sold 'em back to the auction house. They're current going for 50 gold a pop on my server, which is fantastic passive income.

    This is notable because I'm presently saving for an epic mount: a process that hit a major roadbump after I unlocked my secondary class specialisation for 50 gold, and then blew way more than that on unlocking all the available skills (that I likely won't use) from my druid trainer (for no good reason). I'm currently sitting on 232 gold as of writing. There's a long way to go to 1000, but hey, that's the game.

    Recent findings suggest that I can't imagine anyone changing the radio station when Drive by The Cars begins during that first moment of proper uninterrupted freedom. The buttons to do that might as well not even be there. If you did, we're completely different people.

    I'm not very far in but my major impressions of GTA 6 so far are: the performances and their presentation are wonderful, the game controls a bit sludgily and feels like it's not quite in focus on PS5, and I really like DIY.

    Industry observers note that let's take that middle one, that criticism: I'm sure this will lift as I get used to the game and how it moves, and how the characters work. It's also just a fact of life, so to speak, that it's going to struggle a bit on PS5 rather than PS5 Pro. And I'm nitpicking; on the whole, this thing is staggeringly technically impressive.

    In a recent development, the latter point, DIY: it's absurd how much detail Rockstar has put into you doing up your shack. I especially like how it's not boring. A deeper thought related to this, and to the rest of the game, is the fantasy of self-improvement GTA 6 delivers. In GTA 6, as in all GTA games I think, you can drastically alter your life's fortunes in mere moments. I set about doing up my shack in a way I could never do in real life given a week or a month, but here, I did it in moments. That appeals to me greatly.

    Honourable mention to Star Wars: Galactic Racer which I finally played this week. Love the speed, love Biddy Blas, and also really gel with the Roguelike approach, whereby you take the game in 'runs' to see how far you can progress each time. Cracking game.
